name: Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome

criteria.description: Postprandial abdominal pain (epigastric), often with nausea and weight loss
Imaging evidence of celiac artery compression by the median arcuate ligament (CTA or MRA)
Celiac artery peak systolic velocity > 200 cm/s on duplex ultrasound with expiration
Exclusion of other causes of chronic abdominal pain (gastroparesis, PUD, pancreatitis)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical triad of postprandial pain, weight loss, and epigastric bruit with radiographic confirmation of celiac artery compression. Diagnosis of exclusion after other causes are ruled out.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Celiac artery compression is seen incidentally in up to 10-25% of asymptomatic individuals; clinical correlation is essential.

pathognomonic.notes: Pain typically occurs 15-30 minutes after eating

common.notes: Bruit may change with respiration; louder on expiration

rare.notes: From celiac ganglion compression affecting gastric innervation
Rare; from ischemic gastric or duodenal ulceration
Extremely rare; if concomitant SMA/IMA disease

laboratory: Routine laboratory tests are typically normal
May show nutritional deficiencies from chronic malnutrition
imaging: CTA: hook-shaped or hooked appearance of proximal celiac artery with post-stenotic dilation
Duplex ultrasound: celiac artery peak systolic velocity >200 cm/s during expiration
MRA: celiac artery compression by median arcuate ligament
Conventional angiography with respiratory maneuvers (gold standard historically)
other: Celiac plexus block may predict surgical response
Gastric emptying study may show concomitant gastroparesis
Tonometry or visible light spectroscopy to detect mucosal ischemia (research)

distinguishingFeatures: Gastroparesis confirmed by scintigraphy showing delayed emptying
Gastroparesis lacks celiac artery compression on imaging
Chronic mesenteric ischemia typically involves SMA/IMA atherosclerosis
Older patient population with cardiovascular risk factors
SMA syndrome shows duodenal compression on imaging
SMA syndrome often associated with thin body habitus or rapid weight loss

redFlags: Severe weight loss suggesting possible malignancy
Signs of acute mesenteric ischemia (severe sudden pain, peritonitis)
Failure to improve after surgical release (consider alternative diagnosis)
references: Kim EN, et al. Median arcuate ligament syndrome: a review. Ann Vasc Surg. 2013;27(1):113-122.
Dunbar JD, et al. Compression of the celiac trunk and abdominal angina. Am J Roentgenol Radium Ther Nucl Med. 1965;95(3):731-744.
Patel B, et al. Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome. StatPearls. 2024.
